analysis.one_liner: Requires public disclosure of federal crop insurance subsidies received by Members of Congress and Cabinet Secretaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee in March 2015 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Agriculture to publish, every year, the names of Members of Congress, Cabinet Secretaries, and their immediate families who receive federally subsidized crop insurance, along with the dollar amounts of their premium subsidies and any federal payouts. It also would have required the private insurance companies that sell crop insurance to disclose the profits (underwriting gains) they earn from the federal program and the business expenses taxpayers cover. The goal was to make it possible for the public to see whether the people writing farm insurance law are benefiting from it.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and voters. Anyone who wants to know how much federal crop insurance money flows to lawmakers, cabinet officials, and their families would have gotten that information by name, every year. Disclosure of insurance companies' profits from the program would also let the public judge whether the public-private crop insurance arrangement is a good deal for taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual public disclosure, by name, of crop insurance premium subsidies and federal loss payments received by Members of Congress, their immediate families, Cabinet Secretaries, their immediate families, and entities where such individuals hold a majority share.

Requires annual public disclosure, by company name, of the underwriting gains private crop insurance providers earn through the federal program and the administrative and operating expenses the federal government pays them.
The bill's title and provisions are directed at hiding of congressional farm subsidies; it amends the Federal Crop Insurance Act to make this information available to the public.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, Cabinet Secretaries, and their families, whose names and subsidy amounts would become public. Private crop insurance companies, whose per-company profits from the federal program would also become public. No new spending or taxes were proposed.

drawbacks.text: The bill is disclosure-only: it would reveal who receives subsidies but does not ban or limit them, so a Member of Congress could continue collecting federal crop insurance money as long as the amount were published.
Publishing the insurance holdings and subsidy amounts of Members' immediate family members raises privacy concerns for spouses and relatives who are not officeholders themselves.
Annual reporting on every private insurance provider and covered individual would add reporting and administrative work for the Department of Agriculture.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill carried little or no fiscal cost and aimed at a straightforward transparency goal: letting the public see, by name, when the people who oversee farm insurance law profit from it. The main costs are the privacy of officials' family members and added reporting work at USDA. Its honest limitation is that disclosure does not itself stop the payments; it only makes them visible. Still, a low-cost sunlight rule of this kind is hard to argue against on the merits, which makes its quiet death in committee notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee in March 2015, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA) introduced the bill on March 4, 2015, joined by four Democratic cosponsors at introduction (Reps. Kind, Slaughter, Connolly, and Grijalva).
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction, March 4, 2015.
On March 23, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management — the last action the bill ever received.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's action history before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill was never matched by a Senate companion in the record, and all five cosponsors were House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private crop insurance companies keep their per-company profits from the federal program out of public view, and any Members of Congress or Cabinet Secretaries who benefit from subsidized crop insurance continue to receive it without public accounting. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's failure except the status quo.

for.name: Reps. Ron Kind, Louise Slaughter, Gerald Connolly, and Raúl Grijalva

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 4, 2015 and sent it to a subcommittee on March 23, 2015; no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Chairman Mike Conaway
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Agriculture (114th Congress)
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill attracted no Republican sponsorship in the record; no one is recorded as opposing it — it simply never moved past the Agriculture Committee.

industries.note: These companies sell federally subsidized crop insurance and earn underwriting gains and reimbursements on the public's dime; the bill would have made each company's program profits and government-paid expenses public. Disclosure is the main tool outside watchdogs have for judging whether that arrangement overpays the industry.

industries.industry: Federal officeholders with farm or crop insurance interests (Members of Congress, Cabinet Secretaries, and their families)
industries.note: The bill's core purpose was to end the practice of collecting federal crop insurance subsidies without public disclosure. For this group, the status quo that preserved anonymity is what the bill's failure protected.

Farmers and ranchers who buy crop insurance were not covered individuals, but greater transparency about how the program's money flows to officials and insurers can build the case for keeping the program solvent and fair for actual producers.
